_comment: v2 = v1 plus the data-driven perfect fix and four hand-authored conditionals that pass the card-example admission test

constraints.description: English comparative (X-er than / more X / bare -er adjective) requires the analytic comparative with méi
constraints.why: tightened twice from measured violations: \b\w+er\b matched after/under/number, then 'more than'/'more or less' matched idiomatic paraphrases; the remaining condition demands more + an adjective word

constraints.description: A SINGULAR English possessor (my/his/her/its) requires a singular-possessor possessive article
constraints.why: full inflection paradigms instead of \bX\w*\b: the greedy form matched däischtere ('those darker') and sent ('sand'), which made the check fire on non-possessives

constraints.description: English conditional would + verb requires the Luxembourgish conditional auxiliary géif-
constraints.why: the source marks irrealis mood; the target must carry the conditional auxiliary

constraints.description: The indefinite pronoun een may NOT open the sentence when English opens with One/someone
constraints.why: positional prohibition: English marks the initial slot, so applicability is source-derived; the card's own example is the starred violation *Ee(n) kann hei net parken

constraints.description: A first-person plural possessor (our) requires the plural-possessor article eis-
constraints.why: decidable half: 'our' has no homophonous singular variant

constraints.description: Third-person plural possessor (their) requires SOME possessive article (their admits both är- and hir- variants, so possessor NUMBER is not decidable for this person)
constraints.why: measured: 52% of this rule's violations contained a possessive article of the other number, and Luxembourgish allows hir- as a variant of är- for 'their' (hirer Zäit = their time), so requiring är- manufactured false violations; the check is weakened to presence-of-possessive and the description states exactly which claim is being made

constraints.description: The source marks perfect aspect; the target must show an auxiliary and a participle.
constraints.why: v1 required ge-prefix or a hand-picked irregular list and an 80-char window; decomposition of 388 violations showed 34.8% DID contain a hu-auxiliary, 26.3% a copula and 14.7% a ge-word, so the verdict was a form-list/window artifact. Window 120, loan-verb participles (-éiert/-iert) and gewiescht/gewuer added. Tense-choice divergences (present + zanter, simple past) remain a real translation-strategy difference and are expected to keep this rule from certifying.

constraints.description: The source marks past perfect; the target must show a past auxiliary plus participle.
constraints.why: the card's own pair is 'they had built' -> 'si hate(n) gebaut'; the auxiliary pattern keeps the (n) variant written in the book.

constraints.description: A subordinate clause with a 2nd person singular subject shows the clitic before 'du'.
constraints.why: book pairs: 'We know that you leave.'->'Mir wëssen, datt s du fortgees.' and 'I don't know when you will arrive.'->'Ech weess net, wéini s du ukënns.' Note the polite register (Dir) is a legitimate alternative rendering of English 'you', so agreement is expected to be partial.

constraints.description: An approximate cardinal plus plural noun is introduced by 'eng' (or an approximative adverb) in Luxembourgish.
constraints.why: book pairs 'approximately 20 people'->'eng 20 Leit', 'with approximately 100 boats'->'mat engen 100 Boter'; the alternates are the approximative adverbs actually used in the corpus (ronn 180 Staaten).

_dropped.LB_ab00cf7fe49b: article-before-proper-name is decidable from the source only through capitalization, and TranslationVerifier.normalize_text casefolds both sides (grammetarl/validator.py:82), so no source pattern can fire post-normalization. The admission test rejected it rather than letting it ship as an untestable constraint. P3 needs case-preserving verification.
